full_text:
Aaron Rodgers is 4-4 in his career against the Falcons. Benny Sieu / USA Today via Reuters Connect
FLOWERY BRANCH, Ga. — Atlanta Falcons cornerback Avieon Terrell was born 10 months before Aaron Rodgers played his first NFL game.
“It’s crazy,” the rookie said. “I’m ready to look at him in his eye.”
That might be a careful-what-you-wish-for situation, Falcons defensive coordinator Jeff Ulbrich said.
“Obviously, Aaron is one of the best quarterbacks to have ever played at this level,” Ulbrich said. “He’s still playing at a very high level. On top of that, I think he’s got an arsenal of weapons at his disposal. Having to go up against a player of Aaron’s magnitude and the players around him from an offensive perspective, it’s a great challenge. It’s one that they’re all super excited about. I’m excited about it as well.”
The 42-year-old Rodgers will be making his ninth career appearance against Atlanta when the Pittsburgh Steelers play the Falcons on Sunday. He is 4-4 and has averaged 311.5 passing yards per game while compiling a 21-2 touchdown-to-interception ratio, which is the second best in NFL history against a single opponent (among quarterbacks with at least 300 pass attempts), according to Next Gen Stats.
“I mean, they’ve got Aaron Rodgers,” Falcons rookie linebacker Kendal Daniels said. “He’s probably one of the smartest guys in the history of the game. It’s crazy playing him in my first game. I’ve never had to go up against a quarterback like this. He controls the tempo of the game. He never lets the game rush him. You have to really be on top of your game.”
Ulbrich was the defensive coordinator and then interim head coach for the New York Jets in 2023 and 2024 while Rodgers was in New York. He has faced Rodgers only once, in Week 6 of the 2022 season, when Ulbrich’s Jets held Rodgers to 246 passing yards in a 27-10 New York win over the Green Bay Packers.
Rodgers is beginning his 22nd professional season Sunday, and he’s a different quarterback than the last time Ulbrich faced him. In the 2022 season, he averaged 7.8 air yards per attempt, which ranked 24th in the league. Last year, he averaged 5.9 air yards per attempt, which ranked 53rd.
The reason seems pretty clear. He is more eager than ever to get the ball out of his hands. His 2.52-second average time to throw was the second-quickest in the league, according to Next Gen Stats. The only player to get the ball out quicker last year was Atlanta’s Tua Tagovailoa, then with the Miami Dolphins, whose average was 2.51 seconds.
Whether the Falcons can make Rodgers uncomfortable Sunday is an open and vitally important question. One of the stories of the offseason in Atlanta was the loss of edge rushers after Jalon Walker tore his ACL and James Pearce Jr. was suspended for the first eight games of the season.
The Falcons will have to make up for those absences on the interior, where Atlanta has added 6-foot-5, 306-pound Maason Smith, 6-6, 326-pound Gervon Dexter and 6-3, 302-pound Da’Shawn Hand to a group that already included Brandon Dorlus, who had 8.5 sacks last season, and LaCale London, who had five.
“I definitely think we are built for that,” said Ulbrich, who added he will emphasize tipped passes more this season because his interior defensive linemen are bigger.
“I think you’re going to see an uptick in that,” he said.
Here are other lingering questions as the Falcons get ready for Week 1:
Taylor, the Falcons’ new right tackle, has been flagged for 31 false starts since he was drafted in 2019, the second most in the league in that time, according to TruMedia. He was flagged twice for it in three preseason drives this year, and the temptation to jump early is going to be high this week against edge rusher T.J. Watt, who has 115 sacks in his nine-year career.
That’s the bad news. The good news is Taylor should be a dramatic upgrade from Elijah Wilkinson, last year’s starter at right tackle, when the ball does get snapped. Wilkinson gave up 21 quick pressures last year, the most in the league, according to Next Gen Stats. Taylor gave up a quick pressure on only 7.2 percent of his snaps in Kansas City, the ninth-lowest rate in the league.
Protecting Cooper Rush, who was promoted to the starting lineup Friday due to an injury to Tagovailoa, against Watt and the rest of the Steelers front seven will be paramount for the Falcons.
In five years under offensive line coach Dwayne Ledford, the Falcons ran almost exclusively wide-zone rushing schemes. With Kevin Stefanski taking over as head coach and Bill Callahan coaching the offensive line, there should be more diversity this year.
“I ran this run scheme in college with (Steve Sarkisian),” running back Bijan Robinson said. “I don’t want to explain too much, but a lot of different things come at you. You really don’t know what we’re going to do, so I really appreciate that.”
The Steelers could be run on last year. They finished the 2025 season 20th in the league in EPA allowed per rush (0.04), according to TruMedia. On top of that, Pittsburgh had the fourth-highest missed-tackle rate in the league last year, according to Next Gen Stats, which could be a good sign for Robinson, who has been in the league’s top two in missed tackles forced each of the last two seasons.
The new run game “has been looking great in practice,” Robinson said, “but now it’s time to go put it in the show. I know for us as an offense we are anxious to put the product to work.”
The rookie wide receiver was all over the field throughout the spring and training camp and is the second-most exciting player on offense behind Robinson. (Drake London and Kyle Pitts are better players. This is more a comment on how dynamic Branch is with the ball in his hands.)
But there’s a difference between getting a rookie a ton of snaps in practice and trusting him on the field, especially early in the season. Branch should be very involved in what I expect to be an expanded screen game in Atlanta, but the 5-10, 180-pounder will have to prove he can run block to stay on the field.
“Our job is to identify what he does really well, put him in those positions and allow him to play really fast,” Falcons offensive coordinator Tommy Rees said.
Terrell is listed as the starter despite being limited by injury much of training camp. Last year’s starter, Billy Bowman Jr., has returned to the practice field this month after tearing his Achilles last season but was ruled out for this week’s game.
“I am ready right now but still getting there, still have to build some confidence with it,” Bowman said.
Veteran Sydney Brown, acquired via trade with the Philadelphia Eagles in the offseason, also continues to get reps at the position, and the Falcons likely will elevate Darnay Holmes from the practice squad to provide depth.
The Steelers were 3.5-point favorites coming into the week, and that number had increased to 6 points thanks to Atlanta’s quarterback uncertainty. Stefanski is 6-5 all-time against the Steelers, including a 2020 playoff win, but all the signs are pointing to Pittsburgh evening up that record this week.

title: Bills at Texans: What to watch in Joe Brady’s debut, plus a prediction DJ Moore’s role, Jim Leonhard’s debut and the matchups that could decide Bills-Texans, plus our Week 1 prediction. Joe Buscaglia 7
summary:

When the Buffalo Bills begin their Week 1 matchup with the Houston Texans, there will be a lot of new.
The most obvious is first-year head coach Joe Brady, the 36-year-old new leader of the Bills who will make his official regular-season debut on Sunday. There may be no bigger test all season for the Bills coach, who will double as offensive play-ca
full_text:
The Bills open a new coaching era Sunday against a Texans defense that overwhelmed Buffalo in last season’s matchup. Timothy T Ludwig / Getty Images
When the Buffalo Bills begin their Week 1 matchup with the Houston Texans, there will be a lot of new.
The most obvious is first-year head coach Joe Brady, the 36-year-old new leader of the Bills who will make his official regular-season debut on Sunday. There may be no bigger test all season for the Bills coach, who will double as offensive play-caller, than facing the Texans’ vaunted defense.
What stands out most from the Bills’ upcoming matchup?
Here’s our Week 1 Bills notebook.
While the world is focused on the strength-on-strength matchup of Josh Allen and the Bills offense against the tormenting Texans defense, don’t be surprised if another matchup ultimately decides this game. The Bills and Texans entered the offseason with a clear task: Revamping their weaker side of the ball. The Texans brought in some new offensive linemen and a new running back, while the Bills changed their entire defensive scheme with first-year defensive coordinator Jim Leonhard.
The Bills played a lot of their base defense in the preseason, so Leonhard hasn’t shown the full gamut of his playbook, and that could be critical heading into this weekend’s matchup. Leonhard is highly regarded around the league for his mind, and some of the defensive looks he used in open practices throughout the summer have made them much more unpredictable on that side of the ball.
Players throughout the locker room are excited to debut the scheme as if they’ve been keeping it a secret all summer, and that shouldn’t be dismissed with a brand-new play caller. While the players on the field will ultimately decide this contest, Leonhard’s approach to attacking the opponent could be a huge edge for Buffalo against a Texans offense still trying to reach a new level.
Even though Leonhard’s debut is compelling, the Bills will inevitably have to choose on Sunday. In last year’s matchup, the sacks and pressures they gave up to Houston were unsustainable. Though too often in that game, left tackle Dion Dawkins and right tackle Spencer Brown were left on an island against the best edge-rushing duo in the NFL, Houston’s Will Anderson and Danielle Hunter. Some of those sacks and pressures were on Josh Allen, but without question, Allen needs more help this time around against this front.
That’s where the Bills come into the contest with a choice, and what they do will be intriguing from a game-planning perspective. The idea of chipping both edge rushers is obvious, though what will be the most effective personnel grouping to do so?
Because of the matchup, we could see a higher percentage of 12 and 13 personnel than in other weeks to get more two- and three-tight-end looks. That would certainly help the tackles get a second set of hands on those edge rushers. The Bills also have the option to have a receiver stay tight to the formation to chip as well in 11 personnel. The bigger the player chipping, the more effective it will be.
The key to making it all go, however, is new Bills No. 1 receiver, DJ Moore. There is no bigger difference in the 2026 Bills offense from what it was the last two years against the Texans than him.
The Texans were unfazed by who the Bills lined up outside at receiver and clogged up the entire intermediate and middle of the field. Now, with Moore on the field, the Bills have an immediate and proven receiver who can win deep — and that can change the entire structure of how the Texans choose to defend them this year.
I wouldn’t be stunned if the Bills try to establish that part of their offense early to help everyone. Moore’s inclusion as one of two receivers in 12 personnel, or as the only receiver in 13 personnel, could make a massive difference and let the Bills use heavier sets to help their tackles far more often.
As the matchup nears, one of the Bills’ defensive focal points is Texans star receiver Nico Collins. Once the promising second-year player Jayden Higgins suffered a season-ending torn ACL, the gap between Collins and the Texans’ next-best receiver grew significantly.
Houston acquired Kayshon Boutte from New England in late August. When the game begins, he will have studied the Texans’ offense for just shy of three weeks. It puts that much more importance on slowing down Collins on Sunday, which is where the Bills’ No. 2 cornerback situation comes into the picture.
The Bills have been evaluating their cornerback depth all summer. There is no debating top cornerback Christian Benford’s ability or his place in that role, but past him, two significant draft investments have their work cut out for them. The Bills’ 2025 first-round pick, Maxwell Hairston, has been named the starter by Brady, though his inconsistent performance this summer has allowed for some speculation about his hold on the job.
The Bills used a second-round pick on rookie Davison Igbinosun, who has progressed steadily since the beginning of training camp. Most interestingly, general manager Brandon Beane didn’t rule out a potential platoon of Hairston and Igbinosun. Nor did Leonhard when asked about his preferred approach at boundary cornerback: one starter versus a platoon strategy.
The specific strengths of Hairston and Igbinosun have to be considered, especially when it comes to defending Collins. Collins is a big, physical receiver who can win at every level of the field. In today’s NFL, teams are very good at getting their top receivers away from a top cornerback in a shadow role against him, so it’s inevitable that Hairston will see some of Collins.
The concern is that Hairston’s biggest weakness, defending receivers with physicality, is a huge part of Collins’ game. Though when Collins tries to get over the top deep, Hairston has the speed to run with him. Igbinosun is the opposite: His top strength is physicality, but he could surrender something deep against quicker receivers and ones adept at making big plays like Collins.
It’s really a catch-22 for the Bills, which makes you wonder if using a platoon to give Collins different looks throughout the game is the right approach, while also giving Hairston and Igbinosun chances to show they deserve a full-time job.
Even with a summer full of trying to figure it out, the Bills came through final cuts without a real, defined answer at punt returner. They tried Ray Davis there, but Davis’ muffed punt and turnover could have been a blessing in disguise ahead of the regular season. Mecole Hardman was somewhat of an option, but they ultimately cut him after an inconsistent camp. That leaves the Bills with plenty of questions at that spot.
However, the closer we get to their Week 1 game, the more it makes sense for the Bills to go with the practice squad’s Greg Dortch as their primary punt returner on Sunday. Their top option outside of Dortch would be Dee Alford or Davis. Since Alford is critical to their defense and there may be little trust in Davis to do the job after his preseason blunder, it all comes back to Dortch.
For one, he is their best and most explosive option. In a game against a fantastic defense that could limit the Bills’ scoring opportunities, having someone who could give them a drive-start advantage is a big asset.
Second, it would give them a natural backup slot receiver to Khalil Shakir, as the Bills don’t have that elsewhere on their 53-man roster. Plus, Brady pointed out that Dortch’s onboarding hasn’t been as steep because the receiver has worked with receivers coach Drew Terrell in the past.
Third, it would let the Bills bring along rookie Skyler Bell slowly as a healthy scratch, with an eye on increasing his role as the year goes on. Bell doesn’t have a special teams role right now, and to dress five receivers, one of them usually needs that functionality.
Don’t be surprised if, when practice squad elevations come down on Saturday, Dortch is one of them.

full_text:
After Caleb Williams cut back on sacks taken last season, the Bears believe he is ready to take another step. Emilee Chinn / Getty Images
Are you a Bears fan? Are you looking for a quarterback metric more important (and, for residents of Chicago, less annoying) than 4,000 passing yards in a season?
Then there’s good news for you in this season-opening edition of What I’m Hearing.
• Lamar Jackson’s contract situation in Baltimore — no hard feeling this time around; • Why Joey Porter Jr. might have to keep waiting for that new contract; • Three signs the Harbaugh Giants really are going to be different; • That Anthony Richardson Sr. trade request: “I don’t think I have to call and say hey it’s off the table. I think it’s understood”; • Cooper Rush this week, Michael Penix Jr. next?; • And much more.
But first, let’s talk about the middle eight …
It’s a term made popular by Bill Belichick, referring to the final four minutes of the first half combined with the first four minutes of the second half. It’s a magical window of time that can, theoretically, swing a football game.
Bears head coach Ben Johnson has put out the (perhaps fanciful) goal of quarterback Caleb Williams completing 70 percent of his passes. Talking heads will remind you each week that Chicago has never had a quarterback throw for 4,000 yards in a season. But inside the Bears, they’re focused primarily on that middle eight.
“If we can play quality football within structure in those moments, I think he’ll make a huge jump,” a Bears source, not authorized to speak with a reporter, told me recently.
The point of the middle eight — as well as the surrounding 52 — is to score points and prevent the other team from doing so. The easiest and most efficient way to do that is keeping the ball in the offense’s hands. This is Williams’ responsibility.
Johnson loves efficiency. An advocate for advanced metrics, he knows the importance of the expected points added statistic. When he took the job in Chicago, he said : “The EPA in the passing game is really one of the most critical factors in determining wins and losses right now.”
Last year Williams ranked No. 21 in the league in EPA/dropback within the middle eight — 0.07, just below the league average of 0.10 and well behind the league leader (Drake Maye, at 0.39).
Just as how Williams improved year to year by taking fewer sacks (from 68 his rookie year to 24 last season), the Bears think he can make an improvement in middle-eight performance.
Johnson and the team have heard all the “regression” talk. History does say that leading the league in turnovers in consecutive years is difficult. And repeating six fourth-quarter comeback victories (seven if you count the playoffs) probably isn’t realistic. But what if the Bears don’t put themselves in that position in the first place?
“I think it’s lazy,” the Bears source said. “You see interceptions and say, ‘You can’t do that again.’ Fourth-quarter comebacks and say, ‘They can’t come back.’ And you’re ignoring all the space in between that can be improved.
“We use it for fuel more than anything.”
If I am disrespecting the game, I apologize. We are two games into the 2026 NFL season, and I’m already thinking about the 2027 offseason.
The 2027 offseason can accurately be described as the Year of the Quarterback Contract, which obviously will be heavily influenced by the remaining 270 regular-season games and subsequent postseason. There will be multiple $60 million-per-year quarterbacks. There may even be a $70 million-per-year quarterback. Baltimore Ravens quarterback Lamar Jackson doesn’t have a contract extension with the only NFL franchise he’s ever known, and he won’t have one by the time Baltimore takes the field Sunday against the Indianapolis Colts. That is not for a lack of trying.
After spending the summer, particularly the past week, talking with league and team sources, all of whom spoke under condition of anonymity to discuss such a sensitive topic, I do not get the sense there is any animus between the team and player. In fact, I would go as far as to say the relationship between Jackson and the team is the healthiest it’s been. My understanding is that both parties have every intention of continuing their work together for years to come.
The 2024 draft class will be up for extensions come the spring, and that includes Drake Maye, Caleb Williams, Jayden Daniels and Bo Nix. Bryce Young and C.J. Stroud will be looking for paydays then, too. What will Sam Darnold command? Can Jalen Hurts get a new deal? What happens when Kyler Murray balls out in Minnesota? Joe Burrow will be four years deep into his contract extension and may be in need of a true-up.
Odds are that all 10 of those players won’t earn major deals this season, but plenty will. The market will rise, and Jackson will benefit with a productive season.
Gone are the (short-lived) days of the fully guaranteed quarterback contract, and Jackson knows that. He’s even joked about it. The Ravens would have no problem making him the highest-paid quarterback in league history, and the two-time (nearly three-time) MVP has earned it.
Gone, too, are the days of trade requests from Jackson. During a contract stalemate in 2023, Jackson publicly requested a trade. Less than two months later, the two sides reached an agreement that made him the highest-paid quarterback in the league on the basis of average annual salary.
It’s difficult to pinpoint why a deal couldn’t be reached this offseason, but it’s not because either side is mad.
“People definitely think there’s beef, but they’re wrong,” a league source said. “In the past, and now.”
Could a deal be struck during the season? That seems unlikely for the simple fact Jackson serves as his own agent. Talking business during a season with Super Bowl aspirations wouldn’t help either side.
Jackson’s 2027 cap hit balloons to an unmanageable $84.3 million. Such a figure applies an incredible amount of pressure on the team, especially when that player has no-trade and no-tag clauses in his contract, as our Jeff Zrebiec properly noted this week. Jackson has long stated his mission is to win the championships that have eluded him so far. He’s also coming into his own as a businessman (he recently added to his portfolio by partnering with a cinematic K-12 learning platform.) It’s bad business for a player with Lombardi taste to occupy so much of the salary cap.
To be clear, this isn’t to say Jackson should, could or will take less money. The Ravens organization doesn’t have a cash-flow problem, and we all have seen ways the cap has been manipulated since the last collective bargaining agreement, allowing teams to spend more cash than cap (something the league may seek to narrow in the next CBA, by the way.) For now, there is always money in Steve Bisciotti’s banana stand.
If the Ravens win the Super Bowl, the vibes will be immaculate and the check will be blank. If it’s a trying year, things may get complicated. But record deal or not as the season begins, one thing is clear: There are no hard feelings between player and team.
It’s Saturday morning, so there is still time to strike a deal, but after many conversations, I have not been overwhelmed with confidence that the Steelers and Joey Porter Jr. will come to an agreement on a new contract before the start of the season.
The two sides finally engaged in talks this week after several months. Before that, there were legitimate questions of whether the Steelers wanted to extend Porter (though it is the Steelers’ MO to wait longer than players think they should, as our Mike DeFabo laid out ). Pittsburgh has a long-standing policy of not doing contracts in season, so there is a real deadline here.

full_text:
Courtland Sutton fails to haul in a pass against the Chargers last season. Sean M. Haffey / Getty Images
ENGLEWOOD, Colo. — Sean Payton touched his thumbs and index fingers together, forming a triangle. To end his final press conference of the 2025 season in late January, the veteran head coach was teaching fundamentals.
“There’s a proper way to catch a football, and most of the time, it’s with your thumbs together, not the other way around,” Payton said. “The other way around, I’m serious, only exists when the ball is below your belly button. Even the deep balls should be caught with your thumbs together. So we have to be better at that.”
The backdrop for Payton’s review of the basics was a recently concluded season in which the Broncos were charged with 37 drops, according to TruMedia, the second-most in the NFL (17 from wide receivers, tied for fifth-most at that position group). They let six more passes slip through their fingers in the playoffs, the most among the 14 teams in the tournament. Three of those came in Denver’s three-point loss to the Patriots in the AFC Championship Game.
The Broncos are entering Monday night’s season opener with arguably their most talented receiving group since Demaryius Thomas and Emmanuel Sanders were catching passes in Denver. Jaylen Waddle, acquired in a blockbuster trade with the Miami Dolphins in March, gives the Broncos a route-running maestro to complement back-to-back 1,000-yard receiver Courtland Sutton. Marvin Mims (fourth year), Troy Franklin (third) and Pat Bryant (second) have big-game experience in Denver’s offense. As does veteran Lil’Jordan Humphrey, who caught a touchdown pass in the playoff win against the Bills and was one of six receivers Denver kept on its initial 53-man roster.
Still, for a team that was on a quest this offseason, as Payton put it, to find the “meat on the bone” when it comes to improving on the margins, reducing the drops is a clear priority. Payton, at season’s end, fired former wide receivers coach Keary Colbert and hired Ronald Curry, a former NFL wide receiver who spent six seasons coaching alongside Payton in New Orleans. Curry, who was Josh Allen’s quarterbacks coach in Buffalo for the past two years, said he began his work with Denver’s receivers in the offseason by “never assuming anything” about how they catch the football.
“You always address the issues, no matter what it is,” Curry said. “So if that was an issue getting here, I feel like, knock on wood, these guys caught the ball excellently all camp, all offseason. We work on it in between drills, as far as those guys catching the ball, if they’re not in on special teams. As a receiver, you’ve got to be able to run and you’ve got to be able to catch, and that’s what we harp on.”
The focus for Curry with the receivers has been on creating game-like scenarios to rep technique and evaluate how they attack the ball. Knowing whether a receiver is right-hand- or left-hand-dominant, or how they alter their fingers when they are crouching to catch the ball, helps personalize the teaching points.
“A lot of guys feel like they catch 100 Jugs (machine passes) and they’re good, but the ball is coming right at ’em,” said Curry, who was drawn to the Denver job for a chance to coach receivers again and the opportunity to reunite with Payton. “So you want to try to put them in positions where they’re catching the ball without burning their legs up. We sit back there, and I’m a former quarterback, and Kyle (Kempt) has been helping us from the quality-control position in throwing these guys the ball and just coming up with different drills that are better game-like (situations). The more you do that, the better, and then you just harp on it. Just like anything, you coach it. Now, you might not get it the first time, but you try it again, and you try it again until it becomes muscle memory, and then you build that confidence and that callus. I think those guys have done that over the last couple of months.”
Another “meat on the bone” target: creating more explosive plays after the grab. Broncos wide receivers in 2025 produced 35.1 percent of their total yardage after the catch, a figure that ranked 19th in the NFL when isolating for that position. The Broncos had 98 yards after the catch over expectation last season, as tracked by Next Gen Stats, which tied for 23rd in the NFL — well behind the league-leading Steelers (460 YACOE). It’s an area where Waddle should make an immediate impact. He ranked eighth among all wide receivers with at least 100 targets from 2022 to 2024 in yards after the catch per reception (5.9). Curry was on the opposite sideline in four matchups with Waddle as an AFC East rival coach the past two seasons, but being on the field with him each day has given the coach a greater appreciation for the uniqueness of Waddle’s traits.
“You admire him from a distance; you see his skill set, but when you see it live and in color every day, man, his transitional skills are excellent,” Curry said.
“There’s really nothing he can’t do. Teams respect his speed, so he uses that to his advantage, and he can stop on a dime. When you can threaten somebody with speed and get a corner to open, and then you ask that same corner to transition, I don’t know that there’s any corner in the league who can transition with him. He’s a route runner. He’s not a lines-on-paper kind of guy. He has a great feel for football and a high IQ, so he knows how to set up the routes he’s using.”
Broncos offensive coordinator Davis Webb said this week that he has been pleased by the consistency he’s seen from the team’s wide receivers as the opener against the Chiefs approaches. Drops have been more isolated occurrences than bunched miscues during the offseason. And while Bryant may have been the breakout player in camp from the group — “I’m excited to see him play,” Curry said — Webb believes they have a deep room of players who can threaten defenses.
“I think the No. 1 thing is that everyone has had really good consecutive days,” Webb said. “All of them have consistently gotten better from OTAs to here. I think a lot of it is Ronald Curry. … There are a lot of good talks he and I get to have because I was (in Buffalo) before him and then he kind of came after me. I’m very blessed RC is here. I think his relatability with the players is noticeable.”
Now, it’s time to see if it will all come together at the thumbs for Denver’s wide receivers in 2026.

Are you a Bears fan? Are you looking for a quarterback metric more important (and, for residents of Chicago, less annoying) than 4,000 passing yards in a season?
Then there’s good news for you in this season-opening edition of What I’m Hearing.

full_text:
After Caleb Williams cut back on sacks taken last season, the Bears believe he is ready to take another step. Emilee Chinn / Getty Images
Are you a Bears fan? Are you looking for a quarterback metric more important (and, for residents of Chicago, less annoying) than 4,000 passing yards in a season?
Then there’s good news for you in this season-opening edition of What I’m Hearing.
• Lamar Jackson’s contract situation in Baltimore — no hard feeling this time around; • Why Joey Porter Jr. might have to keep waiting for that new contract; • Three signs the Harbaugh Giants really are going to be different; • That Anthony Richardson Sr. trade request: “I don’t think I have to call and say hey it’s off the table. I think it’s understood”; • Cooper Rush this week, Michael Penix Jr. next?; • And much more.
But first, let’s talk about the middle eight …
It’s a term made popular by Bill Belichick, referring to the final four minutes of the first half combined with the first four minutes of the second half. It’s a magical window of time that can, theoretically, swing a football game.
Bears head coach Ben Johnson has put out the (perhaps fanciful) goal of quarterback Caleb Williams completing 70 percent of his passes. Talking heads will remind you each week that Chicago has never had a quarterback throw for 4,000 yards in a season. But inside the Bears, they’re focused primarily on that middle eight.
“If we can play quality football within structure in those moments, I think he’ll make a huge jump,” a Bears source, not authorized to speak with a reporter, told me recently.
The point of the middle eight — as well as the surrounding 52 — is to score points and prevent the other team from doing so. The easiest and most efficient way to do that is keeping the ball in the offense’s hands. This is Williams’ responsibility.
Johnson loves efficiency. An advocate for advanced metrics, he knows the importance of the expected points added statistic. When he took the job in Chicago, he said : “The EPA in the passing game is really one of the most critical factors in determining wins and losses right now.”
Last year Williams ranked No. 21 in the league in EPA/dropback within the middle eight — 0.07, just below the league average of 0.10 and well behind the league leader (Drake Maye, at 0.39).
Just as how Williams improved year to year by taking fewer sacks (from 68 his rookie year to 24 last season), the Bears think he can make an improvement in middle-eight performance.
Johnson and the team have heard all the “regression” talk. History does say that leading the league in turnovers in consecutive years is difficult. And repeating six fourth-quarter comeback victories (seven if you count the playoffs) probably isn’t realistic. But what if the Bears don’t put themselves in that position in the first place?
“I think it’s lazy,” the Bears source said. “You see interceptions and say, ‘You can’t do that again.’ Fourth-quarter comebacks and say, ‘They can’t come back.’ And you’re ignoring all the space in between that can be improved.
“We use it for fuel more than anything.”
If I am disrespecting the game, I apologize. We are two games into the 2026 NFL season, and I’m already thinking about the 2027 offseason.
The 2027 offseason can accurately be described as the Year of the Quarterback Contract, which obviously will be heavily influenced by the remaining 270 regular-season games and subsequent postseason. There will be multiple $60 million-per-year quarterbacks. There may even be a $70 million-per-year quarterback. Baltimore Ravens quarterback Lamar Jackson doesn’t have a contract extension with the only NFL franchise he’s ever known, and he won’t have one by the time Baltimore takes the field Sunday against the Indianapolis Colts. That is not for a lack of trying.
After spending the summer, particularly the past week, talking with league and team sources, all of whom spoke under condition of anonymity to discuss such a sensitive topic, I do not get the sense there is any animus between the team and player. In fact, I would go as far as to say the relationship between Jackson and the team is the healthiest it’s been. My understanding is that both parties have every intention of continuing their work together for years to come.
The 2024 draft class will be up for extensions come the spring, and that includes Drake Maye, Caleb Williams, Jayden Daniels and Bo Nix. Bryce Young and C.J. Stroud will be looking for paydays then, too. What will Sam Darnold command? Can Jalen Hurts get a new deal? What happens when Kyler Murray balls out in Minnesota? Joe Burrow will be four years deep into his contract extension and may be in need of a true-up.
Odds are that all 10 of those players won’t earn major deals this season, but plenty will. The market will rise, and Jackson will benefit with a productive season.
Gone are the (short-lived) days of the fully guaranteed quarterback contract, and Jackson knows that. He’s even joked about it. The Ravens would have no problem making him the highest-paid quarterback in league history, and the two-time (nearly three-time) MVP has earned it.
Gone, too, are the days of trade requests from Jackson. During a contract stalemate in 2023, Jackson publicly requested a trade. Less than two months later, the two sides reached an agreement that made him the highest-paid quarterback in the league on the basis of average annual salary.
It’s difficult to pinpoint why a deal couldn’t be reached this offseason, but it’s not because either side is mad.
“People definitely think there’s beef, but they’re wrong,” a league source said. “In the past, and now.”
Could a deal be struck during the season? That seems unlikely for the simple fact Jackson serves as his own agent. Talking business during a season with Super Bowl aspirations wouldn’t help either side.
Jackson’s 2027 cap hit balloons to an unmanageable $84.3 million. Such a figure applies an incredible amount of pressure on the team, especially when that player has no-trade and no-tag clauses in his contract, as our Jeff Zrebiec properly noted this week. Jackson has long stated his mission is to win the championships that have eluded him so far. He’s also coming into his own as a businessman (he recently added to his portfolio by partnering with a cinematic K-12 learning platform.) It’s bad business for a player with Lombardi taste to occupy so much of the salary cap.
To be clear, this isn’t to say Jackson should, could or will take less money. The Ravens organization doesn’t have a cash-flow problem, and we all have seen ways the cap has been manipulated since the last collective bargaining agreement, allowing teams to spend more cash than cap (something the league may seek to narrow in the next CBA, by the way.) For now, there is always money in Steve Bisciotti’s banana stand.
If the Ravens win the Super Bowl, the vibes will be immaculate and the check will be blank. If it’s a trying year, things may get complicated. But record deal or not as the season begins, one thing is clear: There are no hard feelings between player and team.
It’s Saturday morning, so there is still time to strike a deal, but after many conversations, I have not been overwhelmed with confidence that the Steelers and Joey Porter Jr. will come to an agreement on a new contract before the start of the season.
The two sides finally engaged in talks this week after several months. Before that, there were legitimate questions of whether the Steelers wanted to extend Porter (though it is the Steelers’ MO to wait longer than players think they should, as our Mike DeFabo laid out ). Pittsburgh has a long-standing policy of not doing contracts in season, so there is a real deadline here.
The 2023 second-round pick is entering the final year of his rookie contract with three solid years on his resume but no All-Pro or Pro Bowl honors. He has three career interceptions and 31 passes defensed, including a career-high 14 last season. Quarterbacks had a…

full_text:
The fight song of the Washington Commanders is returning to lyrics used in the past. Brad Mills / USA Today Sports
The horns blared moments after rookie running back Robert Henry Jr. burst into the end zone and Drew Stevens booted the extra point. As the Washington Commanders’ kicking unit jogged off the field just before halftime of their preseason opener against the Miami Dolphins, the large video board at Northwest Stadium flickered with burgundy and gold lights and panned to the crowd. Then, in bold lettering, the lyrics to the team’s fight song flashed across the screen as fans erupted in song.
Hail to the Commanders! Hail vic-tor-y!
Braves on the warpath! Fight for old D.C.!
Run or pass and score, we want a lot more!
Beat ’em, swamp ’em, touchdown! Let the points soar!
Fight on! Fight on! Til you have won!
All of Washington! Rah! Rah! Rah!
Hail to the Commanders! Hail vic-tor-y!
Braves on the warpath! Fight for old D.C.!
Four years after removing the line “Braves on the warpath!” to better align with their new name, the Commanders quietly brought it back — so quietly that most fans that night appeared oblivious to the change.
“I watched fans struggle with (the previous version) a little in the stadium,” team president Mark Clouse told The Athletic shortly after the preseason opener. “And so in the offseason, I said, well, let’s go back and what if we use the old cadence and figure out how many words we can use and kind of let it live.”
Combined with other changes the franchise has made in recent years in an effort to honor its past, the alteration to the fight song renewed speculation that Washington may be intentionally inching closer to its former Redskins brand.
A Commanders spokesperson said the team has not changed its position on returning to its old name. The changes, though, have rankled some in the Native American community.
For decades, the team and its former owner, Daniel Snyder, resisted calls to change that name, which many consider derogatory toward Native Americans.
In 2020 — following the murder of George Floyd and after some of the team’s top sponsors threatened to sever ties with the franchise — Snyder agreed to drop the old moniker and search for a new identity. The team temporarily adopted “The Washington Football Team” before unveiling the Commanders name, with a new logo and uniforms, in February 2022.
During the two-year search for a new brand identity, former team president Jason Wright said that after having discussions with Native American leaders, the franchise believed cutting all ties to Native American imagery “ is the right path .” He added that “an embrace of potentially Native-adjacent iconography and imagery would not represent a clear departure that many communities have so forcefully advocated for us to embrace, and that frankly, we set out to do when we started this process.”
With the new name, “W” logo and uniforms, the team also altered its fight song, via fan vote. “Fight for the Commanders” replaced the line “Braves on the warpath,” and “All of Washington” replaced “Sons of Washington.”
The Commanders’ new ownership group, led by managing partner Josh Harris, purchased the team for a record $6.05 billion in 2023 and quickly made it clear the old name would not return. Wright left the team the following summer. The ownership group fully committed to the Commanders’ name after the team’s successful 2024 season, when it returned to the NFC Championship Game for the first time in more than three decades.
“I think it’s now being embraced by our team, by our culture, by our coaching staff. And so, we’re going with that,” Harris said of the Commanders name in February 2025.
But Harris, along with a number of his 20 limited partners, grew up in the D.C. area as fans of the team when it was winning Super Bowls and dominating the region’s sports culture, and felt it was important to find ways to “honor” the franchise’s past.
“Well, I lived through our past,” Harris said in March. “… I was there for the ’70s, ’80s and early ’90s and so I lived through how amazing those teams were and what an impact it had on me. I know that thousands of our fans, or millions maybe, feel the same way. I think it’s important to go back to that as much as you can. But at the same time, we have a bright future ahead.”
So, over the last two years, the team has brought back its signature gold pants; revealed plans to build a new statue in honor of late safety Sean Taylor; installed an in-stadium tribute to Walter “Blackie” Wetzel, the designer of its old logo; named its draft room in Ashburn after late former general manager Bobby Beathard; adopted the slogan “Raise Hail,” in reference to the song lyrics; unveiled plans to build a new stadium on the site of the old RFK Stadium in D.C. with many of the same aesthetic features of the former venue; changed the uniforms back to what the team wore for throughout its Super Bowl-winning years; developed an alternate helmet with a spear logo that it has dubbed “The Hail Raiser;” and retired the jerseys of Washington legends Darrell Green and Art Monk. The franchise will do the same for John Riggins this season, and Riggins also rejoined the franchise as part of its preseason broadcast team. Clouse announced the news during a training camp practice with Riggins by his side, wearing a blazer that had the old Redskins logo stitched on the inside .
Then, earlier this summer, the team sold a limited set of merchandise online and in its team store that featured some former players and included the team’s old name and logo — a move the team said was done in part to maintain its trademark registration.
“The legal doctrine is called abandonment and basically it says that if you don’t use a mark for three years in a row, the law presumes that you’ve abandoned your rights to that mark and it’s free for others to use,” said Darius Gambino, an intellectual property litigator and partner at Saul Ewing LLP. “So that three years of non-use becomes a point at which you either have to continue using a mark or you have to basically abandon it and give it over for anyone else to use.”
The trademarks for Redskins, Washington Redskins and the logo that features the profile of a Native American are owned by Pro-Football, Inc., the holding company that owns the Commanders (the holding company was renamed Pro-Football, LLC, after Harris purchased the team). Its registration of the marks expires in 2028, but it can file for renewal as early as next year, according to the United States Patent and Trademark Office’s records.
Doing so requires the team to submit an example of the mark in use on the goods or services for which it is registered, Gambino said.
The Redskins merchandise quickly sold out online, but some apparel is still available in the stadium team store, reinforcing the popularity of the old brand while also raising concern from some Native American advocacy groups.
The Association on American Indian Affairs said in a statement that it “condemns the sale of merchandise by the Washington Commanders bearing the former racist team name and Native imagery.”
The organization added, “Native Peoples’ diverse cultures are not brands to be retired and then revived when there is money to be made. The renewed commercialization of Native stereotypes is part of a broader pattern of disrespect toward Native Peoples at a time when Native Nations are fighting very real threats to their sovereignty, cultures, lands, and sacred places. Reviving harmful imagery — that has been proven to harm Native youth — for nostalgia and profit only perpetuates the stereotypes Native Peoples have spent decades demanding be left behind. And, that the sponsors of the Washington Commanders have said should be left behind. Native Peoples have been clear, consistent and unwavering: We are not your mascot.”
It’s fairly common for major organizations that undergo a rebranding to retain the trademarks of their previous brand so others can’t…

title: Ex-Cardinals Pass Rusher Suspended By NFL
full_text:
ARIZONA — Former Arizona Cardinals pass rusher Xavier Thomas is being suspended by the NFL for three games according to the league's transaction page.
It's unclear exactly why he was suspended.
Thomas most recently played with the San Francisco 49ers this preseason before being waived with an injury designation on Aug. 22. He's currently a free agent.
Thomas initially began his NFL career as a fifth-round pick by Arizona in 2024. He played in 14 games his rookie season and pieced together ten total tackles, one pass defensed, one forced fumble and 2.5 sacks.
“I thought he played (with a) high motor and high effort which is really good to see. I saw violence out there and I think he rushed pretty good," former Cardinals head coach Jonathan Gannon said after Thomas' first taste of NFL action.
"He was definitely back around the mix. He caught my eye. He will have a lot to learn out there too. It was good to see him riled up and playing.”
The arrow appeared to be pointing up for Thomas entering 2025, though a mix of poor play (four games and no box score stats) on top of injury returns from BJ Ojulari and Baron Browning squeezed Thomas out of the picture. He was released on Nov. 28.
The Houston Texans picked Thomas up on Dec. 3 and placed him on their practice squad. He eventually signed a futures contract with the team but was waived with an injury designation on May 13.
Now, his future in the league unfortunately appears to be up in the air — especially if we don't know exactly what he was suspended for.
The Cardinals currently have Josh Sweat, Zaven Collins, Baron Browning, Jordan Burch and Eku Leota in their edge room entering 2026.

title: Jeremiyah Love Headlines Final Cardinals vs Chargers Week 1 Injury Report
full_text:
ARIZONA — The Arizona Cardinals and Los Angeles Chargers have unveiled their final Week 1 injury reports leading into the weekend.
For the Chargers, Deane Leonard (abs) is out after not practicing all week while Tuli Tuipulotu (hip) is questionable after being limited all three practice days.
RJ Mickens (ankle), Khalil Mack (rest), Keaton Mitchell (hamstring) and Brenan Thompson (hip) are cleared from the report and are good to go.
Meanwhile, the Cardinals' side of the report was headlined by rookie running back Jeremiyah Love, who is questionable with his ankle sprain after practing in limited fashion all week.
Isaiah Adams (knee), Dadrion Taylor-Demerson (ribs) and Garrett Williams (Achilles) were ruled out by the Cardinals.
Blake Gillikin (groin), Will Johnson (ankle) and Josh Sweat (rest/knee) were removed and are good to go.
Love is nearing recovery from a preseason ankle sprain suffered against the Las Vegas Raiders after tallying 14 touches in one half.
The initial feedback from Arizona wasn't overly concerning from head coach Mike LaFleur, who insisted it was a minor injury. However, Love's injury progressed over time, and he didn't feature in any of the Cardinals' final two preseason games.
Reports throughout the week indicated Love is likely to play, though when speaking with reporters, LaFleur said it was fair to call Love a game-time decision on Sunday.
Love has dazzled and met expectations thus far for a third overall pick, piecing together highlight plays in training camp/preseason.
Cardinals running backs coach Matt Merritt says more time on task will simply help Love be better.
"I think with anything else, the more reps you get, the slower the game becomes. The more you realize the speed at this level is different. I think he's done a really good job of taking the coaching points, whether it's from myself or from Mike [LaFleur] or even from the older guys, and just really taking it to the field understanding [it]," he said.
"Being grounded in the run game, being decisive in the run game at this level is so much more crucial because of how fast everybody is, how fast those holes open and close. I think the progression from that standpoint has gotten much better, and he's got a really good feel for that."
Inactives for Sunday will be 90 minutes ahead of kickoff at SoFi Stadium, though we should learn sooner if Love is trending towards playing or not.

title: Cardinals' 2026 Plan for Carson Beck Is Pretty Revealing
full_text:
ARIZONA — The Arizona Cardinals enter their regular season opener with Carson Beck's development near the top of their mind.
Even if he's not a starter.
The third-round rookie played in one preseason game before suffering a rib injury, one that kept him out for Arizona's final three preseason games. Beck is Arizona's QB3 on the depth chart behind Jacoby Brissett and Gardner Minshew to begin the regular season.
That likely won't be the case once the dust settles on 2026, as the Cardinals need to see Beck play at some point before making a huge decision at quarterback this coming offseason.
That's the buzz online surrounding the team, and while it's not clear exactly how much we'll see Beck this season — the Cardinals are obviously investing in their rookie quarterback.
Cardinals head coach Mike LaFleur met with reporters this week and opened up on Beck's development plan:
"I told you guys I would tell you. So typically, not all the time but typically, the backup quarterback who is Gardner [Minshew] gets all the the look-squad reps if you will. So 32 [reps] on Wednesday, 36 on Thursday, 20 on Friday. Obviously, you don't practice on Saturdays. With our situation, we're splitting it up, making sure that Carson is connected with it," he said.
"Regardless even if we had not done that, the other thing that we do is with those potential inactives, the practice squad guys, the guys that just don't get a ton of reps with their side after practice, they have a 5-10 minute window where in Carson's case he can spot throw through the [game] script and stuff like that.
"So try to keep him connected. As we know, you're one or two plays away from being a guy. So you got to keep them connected with that and continue their development."
You often hear reps are gold in the NFL. Beck played just one game and hasn't seen live action since. Once the regular season arrives, practice reps are mostly allocated to starters with backups not seeing much action.
For Beck to cut into Minshew's workload as a secondary option is fairly telling — not on Minshew, but rather the Cardinals' intentions on wanting Beck to be as prepared as possible for if/when the time comes for him to take the field. Both Brissett and Minshew have been named possible trade candidates for when the midseason deadline arrives.
"It's one of those things, and we talked to Gardner. We've communicated with him. Gardner's played a lot of football, and Carson hasn't in the NFL," LaFleur continued.
"And so, as you're trying to develop these guys, we just thought it was right to do that. Had Gardner been a second-year guy and was our number two, then probably wouldn't be doing this. But because he has played so much football, so much meaningful football in this league, [he] understands this system. Obviously, took all the reps through OTAs, took a ton of reps in training camp. That's why we felt comfortable being able to do this."
Beck won't play in Week 1. Even if Brissett goes down early in 2026, Minshew just might be their guy.
However, all signs point to Beck gearing up for some sort of action this season.

title: Cardinals Say Jeremiyah Love Will Be Last-Minute Call vs. Chargers
full_text:
TEMPE — The Arizona Cardinals are doing their best to downplay running back Jeremiyah Love and his potential to play on Sunday against the Los Angeles Chargers.
"Still got another good day of work today to kind of figure that out. But he's trending well," said Cardinals head coach Mike LaFleur on Friday.
When asked if it was fair to call Love a game-time decision on Sunday, LaFleur said:
Several reports indicate the expectation is Love will play at SoFi Stadium, making his official NFL debut. The Cardinals will reveal game designations later today that will see Love marked as questionable, doubtful, out or fully off the injury report in general.
Official inactives will be due 90 minutes prior to kickoff on Sunday.
Love is working his way back from a high ankle sprain initially suffered in preseason play. Sunday will be two days shy of a full calander month of recovery time for the third overall pick.
Love has been spotted working at practice and his been listed as limited in both prior days of Cardinals practice. LaFleur did rule out starting right guard Isaiah Adams alongside Garrett Williams and Dadrion Taylor-Demerson.
There's been plenty of discussion around the Cardinals' usage of Love and what things will look like in terms of a workload. LaFleur, when speaking with reporters, says regardless of the rookie's health there's always going to be a split workload:
"I think the backs in some aspects are limited anyways because we're going to sub them. I don't really care if everyone was 1000%, I don't believe in playing those guys 65 of the 65 snaps, or 72 of the 72 snaps," he said.
"So we'll always do what we think is best for these guys, health-wise, first and foremost. And then second, what's going to help us as a team."
Love's playmaking out of the backfield, though only seen live in one game during preseason, was fairly obvious — which has generated plenty of buzz around the desert. Some aren't fans of how the Cardinals will deploy Love, at least initially, though LaFleur seems insistent to not run any of his running backs into the ground.
That makes sense in terms of health, though Arizona also likes what they have out of power runner Tyler Allgeier and third rotational rusher Bam Knight. James Conner is on injured reserve and is eligible to return after four weeks as well.

title: Cardinals Already Forced to Make Lineup Change vs Chargers
full_text:
ARIZONA — The Arizona Cardinals are already ruling out starting right guard Isaiah Adams ahead of their Week 1 matchup against the Los Angeles Chargers.
Head coach Mike LaFleur told reporters Adams would miss action at SoFi Stadium on Sunday. Dadrion Taylor-Demerson and Garrett Williams were also ruled out.
Jon Gaines will fill in for Adams, according to LaFleur. Gaines is the first-choice backup in the interior for either guard or center.
"He's played a lot of football. I think Gaines is a really good football player, and he's got the look in his eye that it's not going to be too big for him," LaFleur told reporters.
"He's had a lot of reps obviously over the last few weeks, it's unfortunate why he had the reps because of Isaiah. But that's ball, so he'll be ready to roll."
The Cardinals previously battled injuries all of last season, especially along the offensive line. That luck (or lack thereof) continues into this season, especially after the team lost second-round pick Chase Bisontis to an MCL injury in preseason play.
The team's official injury report will be released later today, though Adams hasn't practiced any of the last two days leading into Friday.
The Cardinals' offense will be facing a new-look Chargers defense with prior coordinator Jesse Minter gone.
"One, it's week one. I mean I get it. He (Chargers Defensive Coordinator Chris O’Leary) wasn't in the league last year and two years ago he was with the Chargers and whatnot. Even if he had been there for 10 years, there's going to be different stuff that they would've done," said LaFleur.
"I'm sure if (Ravens Head Coach) Jesse (Minter) was still there that there was going to be adjustments probably made, so you've always got to be prepared for that. You go off of what you see from tape, you talk about their players and what they do well, but most importantly it's about us and I'm sure they're saying the same stuff. The first few weeks it's about what you do, how you execute and how you go about your business, and then understanding that you've got to be able to adapt based on what they're doing."
Now, Arizona will be tasked with attacking that defense without their starting right guard entering Los Angeles.

title: Injury Report: Cardinals Trending Toward Losing Starter for Week 1 vs Chargers
full_text:
ARIZONA — Thursday saw the return of Arizona Cardinals edge rusher Josh Sweat, who took the field for the first time in the 2026 regular season after taking a rest day on Wednesday.
Sweat, alongside the continued participation of rookie running back Jeremiyah Love, highlights the Cardinals' side of the injury report — though starting right guard Isaiah Adams was once again absent.
Before diving into Arizona's side of Thursday's injury report, here's Los Angeles' portion:
FULL - RJ Mickens (ankle), Khalil Mack (rest)
LIMITED - Keaton Mitchell (hamstring), Brenan Thompson (hip), Tuli Tuipulotu (hip)
Mickens and Mack were the only two players who saw a change of status from Wednesday in Los Angeles — both improving from their limited and DNP designations, respectively. Leonard missed a second straight day, which doesn't bode well for his status entering the weekend.
When speaking with Chargers reporters, quarterback Justin Herbert offered plenty of praise ahead of his matchup with Budda Baker.
"He does everything. He's able to make so many plays in so many different positions on the field and they kind of let him do his thing and that's what he does best," Herbert said of Baker.
"He goes and makes plays and whether he's in the run fits, dropping back coverage, he just finds a way to be around the ball and he's definitely going to have to be aware of on the field."
FULL - Blake Gillikin (groin), Will Johnson (ankle)
LIMITED - Jeremiyah Love (ankle), Garrett Williams (Achilles), Josh Sweat (rest/knee)
DNP - Isaiah Adams (knee), Dadrion Taylor-Demerson (ribs)
Adams' status is looking doubtful for Sunday, along with backup safety Taylor-Demerson after being downgraded on the team's injury report.
Adams was expected to compete with Chase Bisontis for the right guard job, which appeared to be close prior to Bisontis' potentially season-ending MCL injury suffered in preseason. That cleared the way for Adams to fully anchor starting duties, though his knee injury has kept him out of practice dating back to last week.
Jon Gaines appears to be in line to start at right guard. The versatile interior player is listed as the No. 2 option at guard and center in Arizona's first depth chart of 2026 while he made five starts last season.
Gaines impressed during preseason and has been waiting to emerge as a full-time starter in Arizona after three seasons, his rookie campaign being cut short due to injury.
Cardinals head coach Mike LaFleur is scheduled to speak with reporters on Friday morning, where he'll provide an update on Adams and other injured players ahead of the weekend.
Arizona will hold one more practice before designating players as out, questionable or doubtful on their Friday injury report.

title: Everyone Is Counting Out the Cardinals — They Don’t Care
full_text:
There's noise outside of the Arizona Cardinals' facility in Tempe.
Aside from birds chirping and ambience of cars commuting from nearby streets, an overwhelming majority of NFL media and fans are down on the Cardinals' chances to play well in 2026.
The prospects of this season don't shake out well. The Cardinals are under a rookie head coach, a bridge quarterback and a shaky defense that didn't improve much on their side of the ball over the course of the offseason. All while having one of the league's toughest strengths of schedule and playing in a highly competitive NFC West.
The path to a postseason, according to most, is a forgone dream. There's already talk about the Cardinals making trades at the midway deadline to prepare for the 2027 season.
Yet nearly 60% of games in the NFL, on average, come down to one possession. Arizona, for as large of underdogs as they are, aren't far behind top teams in the league.
That's reality, at least for now when records are 0-0.
"No, we're not concerned about the noise," head coach Mike LaFleur said at his Wednesday press conference.
Much of the excitement around the Cardinals and their potential to play spoiler this season rests on the shoulders of LaFleur, who hails from prestigious offensive minds. Arizona took a massive swing at the plate with another first-time coach running the show, though his potential to be the next premier play-calling head coach is legitimate.
His quarterback in Jacoby Brissett also echoed a similar sentiment when asked if it matters if they're considered underdogs.
"Nope. Zero," he said before being asked what he wants to prove this season:
"It's literally not about me. I want to go out there and win. The guys in the locker room want to go out there and win, and I think that's our main focus."
Brissett's capable of running LaFleur's offense, having a quick ability to diagnose defenses and spread the ball around to pristine playmakers without turning the ball over often. Out of a quarterback in LaFleur's offense, that's all you can ask for out of Brissett.
The biggest question mark resides on the defensive side of the ball, where coordinator Nick Rallis was brought back for a fourth season. Quite honestly his unit has numerous strides to make if the Cardinals will be competitive, and it's possible he's on the hot seat entering 2026.
“Ignore the noise. We’re focused on what do we have to do right now to get ourselves prepared for Sunday," Rallis told reporters.
“Ignore the noise. We’re focused on what do we have to do right now to get ourselves prepared for Sunday.” Arizona Cardinals DC Nick Rallis isn’t paying attention to what people are saying about the defense going into the season. pic.twitter.com/6OQpBo3thK
"There a lot of things externally that do matter to people, and everyone's got different stuff. Career aspirations or money or just outside perspective and reputation. So it is a real thing, but at the end of the day the result we want is to win games, and in order to win games you got to play good defense," said Rallis.
"So the best way to go about that is, where do we hold our attention in the moment? If we're putting our attention on anything but preparing for the Chargers, it's going to take us away from maximizing that opportunity on Sunday. Easier said than done, but that is 100% of what this building is about — being where your feet are and attacking whatever we're in —  meetings, walk-through, practice, recovery, all of that."
There's sure a lot of belief within the Cardinals' building, as it should be. Whether it's a mistake or not for everybody else outside of those walls is entirely up to their performance.

title: Cardinals Trade Rumors: Is Jacoby Brissett on the Move?
full_text:
The Arizona Cardinals probably won't be a team to watch on a national level week to week, though their quarterback situation sure might dominate headlines.
The Cardinals pulled the plug on Kyler Murray this offseason, placing them into quarterback purgatory. Journeyman Jacoby Brissett leads the way while veteran backup Gardner Minshew and rookie third-round pick Carson Beck sit behind.
The overall sentiment, thanks to a tough schedule and first-year head coach in Mike LaFleur , is Arizona will eventually trot out multiple quarterbacks through the course of the regular season.
There could even be a trade, according to ESPN NFL insider Jeremy Fowler:
"Arizona's quarterback situation is underplayed, possibly because of the Cardinals' perceived noncontender status and Carson Beck being a third-round pick. But they absolutely have enough talent to move the ball, and Brissett averaged 280.5 passing yards per start over 12 games last season," Fowler said.
"If Brissett plays well but the Cardinals struggle to win, he could be a trade candidate at midseason. That opens a path for Arizona to see what it has in Beck, who acquitted himself well in the preseason, before considering their 2027 draft options."
The potential of trading a quarterback, at least in the desert, is nothing new. We previously broke down the possibility of trading Minshew midseason with Beck waiting in the wings.
That would make sense, though this also isn't the first time Brissett's name has been tossed around in trade rumors. One NFL general manager previously told Jason La Canfora he was confident Brissett would be traded.
“They’ll move Brissett by the deadline,” the general manager said. “Watch.”
Brissett recently had his deal reworked to have $15 million guaranteed on his contract with a void year in 2027.
Teams, especially those looking to make a playoff push, are always looking to bolster their quarterback room around the deadline. Injuries unfortunately happen to anybody and everybody, and if a big name goes down, the Cardinals would be a prime candidate for outside teams to work with on a quarterback trade.
As Fowler alluded to, Arizona needs to see Beck as much as possible this season before making a massive decision on what they'll do at quarterback following 2026. Clearing that path by trading either of Brissett or Minshew — both of whom are set to be free agents after this year — would make the transition to Beck easier.

title: 3 Most Important Things Mike LaFleur Said About Cardinals vs Chargers, and Why They Matter
full_text:
The Arizona Cardinals are putting the final touches on their Week 1 game plan against the Los Angeles Chargers, and it's finally football season in the desert.
Truth be told, there's so much unknown as we approach Sunday. That can be either good or bad, depending on how you slice it.
Head coach Mike LaFleur shared a few words at his weekly press conference — here's the three most important things, and why they matter:
LaFleur on Tyler Allgeier Being Listed Above Love: "You know the answer to that — but I appreciate the question. I really do. But no, don't look too far into that."
Why it Matters: The Cardinals were always going to run a 1A/1B approach at running back with Tyler Allgeier and Jeremiyah Love, though eyes were raised when Love (the third overall pick) was placed as a secondary option. The reality is Love is working his way back from injury — but even when fully healthy, he's not going to be a workhorse back.
LaFleur on Williams' Plan This Week: "We're going to take that all the way up into the weekend. We want to make sure he feels as good as he can. I think there's a return to play and a return to performance, and you got to lean on the player for that second part. A guy like Garrett, he is as real as they come. So, if he's ready to roll, he'll be ready to roll. And if he needs a little bit more time, then we'll go that way."
LaFleur on Denzel Burke Stepping Up in Slot: "I think all three are capable. I'm not going to limit them saying they're not because well, I haven't seen Will [Johnson] do it. I think if we trained him there, he would. But when we thought, what is the best — if we have to have the nickel pass coverage out there — what is the best way to go about it? And that is what we all kind of thought, keep Max [Melton] and Will outside, move Denzel inside. Three guys that you have a lot of trust in, no matter where they're at."
Why it Matters: Williams is slowly working his way back from injury and appears to be a true 50/50 call entering the weekend. His placement as a backup, similar to Love, is indicative of health more so than performance. If he can't go, it's interesting Burke would slide into the slot as opposed to Melton, who has previous experience doing so.
LaFleur on Preparing For Week 1 Facing New Coordinators: "You go off what you see from tape. You talk about their players and what they do well, but most importantly, it's about us. And I'm sure they're saying the same stuff. This first week, the first few weeks, it's about what you do and how you execute, how you go about your business, and then understanding that you know you got to be able to adapt based on what they're doing."
Why it Matters: With little game-planning to do, execution is the name of the game in the early stages of the league season. That's always the case, though with little film available, there's more of an emphasis on internal operation. We'll see exactly how much the Cardinals have digested LaFleur's offense and Nick Rallis' updated defense.

title: Sam Darnold Injury News Completely Changes Seahawks vs Cardinals
full_text:
ARIZONA — The Arizona Cardinals are set to host the Seattle Seahawks in Week 2 action at State Farm Stadium, though the NFC West matchup just had a massive wrench tossed into the works.
In the regular season opener, Seahawks quarterback Sam Darnold went down early in the first quarter and quickly was ruled out for the rest of the game with a hip injury. Drew Lock filled in for the defending Super Bowl champions and guided the Seahawks to a 13-10 win.
Darnold, with initial fears of a long-term injury, had an MRI done this morning with some positive news in terms of his outlook for the season. ESPN NFL insider Adam Schefter said , "team doctors still are reviewing to determine how much time he will miss. It is expected to be some, but for now the team believes it, as one source described, 'dodged a bullet.'"
And if you're wondering — yes — Darnold is slated to miss their battle against the Cardinals in Week 2.
Sam Darnold is expected to miss next week's game, but he should be back sooner, rather than later, sources say. Could be just a few weeks. With 17 days from Wed. until their Week 3 game against the #Commanders , Darnold gets a schedule break, as well. https://t.co/UjGk85IYPA
And that completely changes the dynamic, even if the Cardinals have yet to play their own regular season snaps.
Darnold was key in getting Seattle a Super Bowl ring last season, running the offense to near perfection and keeping things on schedule with weapons around him. That story wasn't supposed to be any different in 2026 with Jaxon Smith-Njigba, Cooper Kupp and Jadarian Price headlining the weapons Seattle has.
Lock stepped in admirably, completing 16-of-22 passes for 187 yards and one touchdown against the Patriots. However, there's a clear drop-off in terms of talent and experience between the two quarterbacks.
Darnold's capable of making clutch throws across the field — Cardinals fans remember that Thursday night game last year where Darnold put Seattle in field goal range to avoid an upset. Not to say Lock isn't capable with a strong rushing attack and sound defense behind him, though the Seahawks are now lacking their leader with their offensive ceiling now feeling limited.
That's good news for the Cardinals, who now have just a tad of game film on Lock after last night and can use that to build a gameplan from. Of course, results are pending from Arizona's own regular season opener when they travel to Los Angeles to face the Chargers on Sunday.
However, a seemingly impossible task of beating Seattle in Week 2 just got a tad less daunting, if Darnold misses action at State Farm Stadium as expected.

title: Falcons vs. Steelers Odds, How to Watch, Injuries for NFL Week 1
full_text:
ATLANTA – The Atlanta Falcons are kicking off the first week of this season with a trip north to face off with the reigning AFC North champion Pittsburgh Steelers. The series has not been kind to the Dirty Birds, and the Steelers lead the all-time series 16-2-1.
The last Falcons win in the series came in 2006, while the other dates all the way back to 1970. Their last matchup also came in a Week 1 debut for a new Falcons head coach – then Raheem Morris – but that ended in an offensive nightmare for Kirk Cousins and the offense.
This Sunday will prove to be another difficult challenge for Atlanta.
After a late-week injury to Tua Tagovailoa and a prolonged recovery for Michael Penix Jr., Kevin Stefanski’s first regular-season game as head coach will be quarterbacked by third-stringer Cooper Rush. The test was already going to be difficult, with the Steelers fielding a star-studded front seven loaded with difference-makers.
T.J. Watt, Cameron Hayward, and Alex Highsmith all return for an elite pass-rushing unit that will be licking its chops to face Rush under center.
“I mean, they've gotten older, but they're certainly still very effective,” Falcons offensive coordinator Tommy Rees said about this test. “They're high motor, high skill level, high intellect. They know what they're doing out there. They’ve played a lot of football.”
The Falcons will face a unique challenge on Sunday , not only because they'll face a top-flight defense but also because they'll face future Hall of Fame quarterback Aaron Rodgers and his former head coach Mike McCarthy. Alongside him, the offense will feature a pair of dangerous wideouts in DK Metcalf and Michael Pittman Jr., plus a strong running back duo in Jaylen Warren and Rico Dowdle.
Falcons defensive coordinator Jeff Ulbrich appreciates the challenge awaiting his defense this week in Pittsburgh.
“Obviously, he's one of the best quarterbacks that has ever played this game, and still playing at a very high level,” he said of Rodgers and the Steelers’ offense. “On top of all of that, I think he's got an arsenal of weapons at his disposal as well: the receiving corps, the tight end group, the two running backs. Then the way that, historically, Coach McCarthy has featured guys with very specific roles and skill sets, it's going to be a great challenge.”
The Falcons have weapons of their own, boasting one of the NFL’s best offensive trios in Bijan Robinson, Drake London, and Kyle Pitts Sr. With the quarterback uncertainty , this group will need to carry a lot of weight for the offense on Sunday.
Here’s everything you need to know to watch Sunday’s Week 1 matchup between the Falcons and Steelers.

title: Falcons Final Injury Report: Tua Tagovailoa, Michael Penix Jr. Among Week 1 Absences
full_text:
The Atlanta Falcons will enter Week 1 against the Pittsburgh Steelers without several key players, including both of their top quarterbacks.
The Falcons released their final injury report Friday, officially ruling out quarterback Tua Tagovailoa with an oblique injury. Tagovailoa had been named Atlanta's starting quarterback earlier in the week, but his status quickly became uncertain after he appeared to be dealing with the injury during Thursday's practice .
With Tagovailoa unavailable, veteran quarterback Cooper Rush will make his Falcons debut as the starter. Rookie Jack Strand will serve as the backup.
Michael Penix Jr. will also miss Sunday's season opener as he continues his recovery from a knee injury. Penix was a full participant Friday, an encouraging sign in his rehabilitation, but he remains unavailable for the Steelers matchup.
The quarterback situation now leaves Atlanta with Rush taking the first-team snaps against Pittsburgh and Strand preparing for his first NFL action if needed.
The Falcons will also be without cornerback Billy Bowman Jr. for the opener. Bowman was limited in Friday's practice while continuing to work his way back from an Achilles injury. The rookie had been ramping up his workload throughout the week, but Atlanta will hold him out of Sunday's game.
Offensive tackle Cameron Williams is another player ruled out. Williams did not participate Friday because of an ankle injury, creating another absence along the offensive line. Williams was added to the team as a waiver-wire addition after initial cutdowns two weeks ago.
One of the biggest remaining questions heading into Sunday involves veteran defensive end Za'Darius Smith. Smith is listed as questionable with a shoulder injury despite returning to full participation Friday. His availability could be significant for a Falcons defense preparing to face Steelers quarterback Aaron Rodgers.
Atlanta did receive positive news elsewhere on the injury front.
Wide receiver Zachariah Branch, linebacker Kendal Daniels, defensive linemen Brandon Dorlus and Da'Shawn Hand, offensive lineman Kyle Hinton, and offensive tackle Jawaan Taylor were all full participants Friday.
Daniels' progression is particularly notable after he dealt with an Achilles injury during the week. He is expected to have a significant role in Atlanta's defensive plans if available.
Left tackle Jake Matthews did not participate Friday, but his absence was listed as not injury-related, as the veteran received a rest day.
The Falcons will now turn their attention toward Pittsburgh, where Rush will lead the offense, and Atlanta will hope Smith can suit up for a defense that has spent the offseason building a more physical front.
